name: Cloud-Herding Body Canon (Mục Vân Thể Kinh)
concept: The founder's method, learned from the herd. The disciple tempers the body on horseback: the long ride, a day and a night at the gallop, one more hour for each layer, until the legs and the spine take the horse's rhythm and keep it on foot. It runs on no element. What it needs is bone and patience, and a horse that will carry the disciple that far. In a fight it is momentum: the holder hits harder the longer they keep striking, and their beast fights beside them in step.
lore: Mẫn Bạch Câu wrote it in 742 from the way the plain's herders had always broken their colts and themselves together. The first page says: a horse is a disciple's first master.

name: Herd Call (Quần Mã Hiệu)
concept: A whistled call, half breath and half qi, that a horse raised on the manor answers from a valley away. The inner disciple learns to call one beast, then three, and the head can turn the whole herd. In a fight it calls a horse to the holder's side and steadies it: the beast's attack and speed rise while it answers the whistle, and fear or slows are cleared.
lore: No book: it is taught by ear, in the stables, in the disciple's first year, and the outer gate is not allowed to hear it.

name: River-Ice Bucket Breath (Hàn Trì Đam Tức Pháp)
concept: A hired groom's working breath, shaped by thirty summers of hauling two buckets of river ice from the plain's creeks to the north paddock's straw. It keeps a Water-and-Wood body steady under load and teaches none of the manor's riding canons.
lore: Hứa Tịch Câu kept his father's Chu Tân ferry cadence in his shoulders and turned it into the rhythm he carries ice by.
